title: Trent opens, 1545
hook: a council that answers the reformers and reforms the Church from within

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas More. Your line was martyrs on both sides. This week went from Lateran IV and Constance to Florence, Luther's theses, the reformers' questions, and England. Now the Church answers. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

Trent is a small city in a valley of the Alps, on the road between Italy and the German lands. That's why it was chosen: a place the emperor's people and the pope's people could both reach and both accept. For years, people on more than one side had called for a council. Popes hesitated, rulers quarreled, wars got in the way. At last the bishops gathered in the cathedral there. Today's word is Catholic Reformation.
screen: `A CITY IN THE ALPS.` → `YEARS OF WAITING.` → `AT LAST, A COUNCIL.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Historians sometimes call this the Counter-Reformation, as if it were only a reaction. Others prefer Catholic Reformation, because reform inside the Church had already started. Ignatius of Loyola, a wounded soldier, had gathered companions who became the Jesuits. Teresa of Avila would soon reform her Carmelite convents back toward poverty and prayer. Trent gathered that energy into one place. Next, the first big choice. The bishops at Trent decided to work on two things side by side: doctrine and discipline. They would answer the reformers' questions about faith, and at the same time fix the Church's own house. Not one or the other. Both. Then, what fixing the house meant. One example: the council insisted that bishops actually live in their dioceses and care for their people, instead of collecting income from far away. That was one of the abuses we heard about two days ago, addressed by the Church's own council. Last, the root. Paul writes in Romans, in the Douay-Rheims, "be reformed in the newness of your mind." In the Latin Bible the word is reformamini: be reformed. For Catholics, reform isn't someone else's word. It's in their own scripture, and it starts with the mind and the heart, not the walls: reform from within. Over the next days we'll follow what Trent actually said.
screen: `CATHOLIC REFORMATION, NOT JUST COUNTER.` · `DOCTRINE AND DISCIPLINE TOGETHER.` · `BISHOPS MUST LIVE WITH THEIR PEOPLE.` · `BE REFORMED IN YOUR MIND.` · then, large: `REFORM FROM WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reform one habit. Not your whole life. One habit. Use the sit. Go back to the reform you named a couple of days ago, or choose a fresh one. Picture the moment the habit usually happens: the time of day, the room, what's in your hand. Now picture yourself doing the better thing instead, once, in that same moment. Keep it small enough that you could actually do it tomorrow. If you pray, you can ask for help to begin. The bell holds the time.
Catholic Reformation. The renewal of the Church from inside, gathered at the Council of Trent, answering the reformers and fixing its own house. Today's word.
Your line: reform from within. Today, before you ask anyone else to change, take the first step of your own one habit. Day seven hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics remember the Council of Trent as the center of the Catholic Reformation; religious orders founded or renewed in that era, like the Jesuits and the Discalced Carmelites, are still active today.

notes: Year 1545 is in the index title only; not spoken. 'For centuries' kept general.
Vulgate Romans 12:2 'sed reformamini in novitate sensus vestri': confirm.
'Trent was chosen as a place both sides could reach' (an imperial city on the Italian side of the Alps): confirm phrasing.
'The opening crowd was small': confirm (small attendance at the opening session).
Decision to treat dogma and reform in parallel (early in the council): confirm session.
Residence of bishops: Trent's reform decrees; the strongest decree came in a later period. Confirm wording 'insisted'.
Ignatius and the Jesuits approved before Trent opened; Teresa's reform began later ('would soon'): confirm.
Week-end review names the week's days (778–783).
